clue.text: Finest possible condition for old coin found in the garden

definitions.text: Finest possible condition for old coin
definitions.meaning: a coin in perfect, unused condition is described with this word by collectors
a common herb grown in gardens

explanation.surface: A collector notes that a perfect old coin was dug up in the garden.
explanation.definitionFit: Numismatists grade an unworn coin with this word, and it is also a common garden herb.

clue.text: Inch from the brink

definitions.meaning: to inch is to move slowly, sidling forward
the brink is the very border of a drop

explanation.surface: Someone shuffles back a little from a precipice.
explanation.definitionFit: To move gradually is to sidle or creep forward, and a border or lip is the same as a brink.

clue.text: Stake but not post

definitions.meaning: a poker player's opening bet
Latin 'before', the opposite of 'post' meaning after

explanation.surface: A wooden stake, someone insists, is not the same as a post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stake' and 'post' look like two lengths of wood; the first is a poker bet and the second the Latin prefix for 'after', whose opposite is 'before'.
explanation.definitionFit: A poker bet placed before the deal, and the Latin prefix meaning 'before', the reverse of 'post'.

clue.text: Take to your heels-don't worry about me go like crazy

parts.note: to take to your heels is to run

indicators.note: about means the reassurance is wrapped around the short form of me

parts.note: A-OK is a reassurance that all is fine
M is the usual abbreviation for me

explanation.surface: Someone tells a friend to flee and not worry about them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'don't worry about me' reads as a plea from someone left behind; A-OK is the American 'all fine', and 'about' wraps it round the M for me.
explanation.definitionFit: To behave wildly and without control is to go like crazy.

clue.text: Doesn't sound like one of the big guns in the church

definitions.text: Doesn't sound like one of the big guns in the church

parts.words: Doesn't sound like one of the big guns in the church
parts.note: the title of a junior cathedral cleric is said exactly like a small piece of artillery, so it sounds like a little gun and not one of the big ones

explanation.surface: A lowly clergyman is not one of the church's heavyweights.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on a cathedral rank whose name is said like 'minor cannon'; 'big guns' means both important people and large artillery.
explanation.definitionFit: A junior member of a cathedral's clergy, below the canons proper, is far from an important figure.

clue.text: Airship heading for pre-Nazi Germany

definitions.meaning: the German zeppelin that burned at Lakehurst in 1937
the field marshal who was president, so head of state, of the Weimar Republic

explanation.surface: An airship sets its course for Germany before the Nazis took power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading' looks like a course being steered; it means being head of state, as Paul von Hindenburg was president of Germany until 1934.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous zeppelin was named after the field marshal who was president of Weimar Germany.

clue.text: Suet pudding swallowed by wedded man occupied by a visitor

indicators.note: swallowed by means the mixed letters go inside the word for the husband

parts.note: a groom is a man just married

indicators.note: a pudding is a mixture, so the letters of suet are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to be mixed

explanation.surface: A bridegroom gulps down a suet pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pudding' looks like the dish itself but signals a mix of the letters, which 'swallowed by' places inside the newly married man.
explanation.definitionFit: A spare bedroom kept for a staying visitor is the one such a guest occupies.

clue.text: Decapitated their son maybe

indicators.note: decapitated means the word their loses its head, its first letter

explanation.surface: Their son was beheaded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decapitated' removes the T at the front of THEIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A son is one example of a successor who will inherit.

clue.text: Waylay or delay

definitions.meaning: to waylay is to rob someone at gunpoint on the road
to delay someone is to make them late

explanation.surface: Ambush or hold back, a highwayman weighs his choices.
explanation.definitionFit: A highway robbery, and also making someone late or keeping them back.

clue.text: Ones indicated here by neat, orderly house in Washington

parts.note: the pronoun for things pointed to nearby

indicators.note: orderly suggests putting things in order, so the letters of neat are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone points out a tidy, well-run house in the US capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neat, orderly' reads as a description of the house; 'orderly' is the signal to rearrange 'neat'. The house is the upper chamber of the US Congress.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper chamber of the US Congress meets in Washington, a legislative house.

clue.text: Take the chair to undergo an examination

definitions.meaning: to take the chair
students ... an exam

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to be seated for a test.
explanation.definitionFit: Being seated is taking a chair, and British students are said to take a test by this verb.

clue.text: T U C leader swallows nothing representing Trotsky

indicators.note: swallows means the union man's name takes the zero inside it

parts.note: Len Murray was general secretary of the Trades Union Congress
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A trade union boss takes on the role of Trotsky.
explanation.walkthrough: The TUC is Britain's Trades Union Congress; Len Murray led it in the 1970s and 80s. 'swallows' puts O inside LEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Trotsky's first name was this, the revolutionary born Lev Bronstein.

clue.text: Low character associated with the turf

definitions.meaning: a British slang insult for an unpleasant person
a piece of grass with its soil

explanation.surface: A shady racing type hangs around the turf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the turf' suggests horse racing; it is literal grass.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a nasty person, and a clod of grass with its roots and earth.

clue.text: Sport in Merseyside

parts.note: read the word sport as S plus port, with S standing for the compass direction, and the place is a seaside town near Liverpool

explanation.surface: A sporting event takes place in Merseyside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sport' looks like games, but split it as S-PORT with S for south, giving a coastal town in Merseyside, the county around Liverpool.
explanation.definitionFit: A resort town on the Lancashire coast, now part of the county of Merseyside, whose name splits as a southern harbour.

clue.text: Can the storm-tossed sur vivers reach it while the flask is not yet empty?

definitions.text: Can the storm-tossed sur vivers reach it while the flask is not yet empty?

parts.words: Can the storm-tossed sur vivers reach it while the flask is not yet empty?
parts.note: shipwreck survivors hope to reach calm seas, and a flask of drinking water still has some left in it

explanation.surface: Shipwrecked sailors wonder if they will reach calm water before their drink runs out.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase has two readings: calm water the survivors want, and drinking water still remaining in the flask.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm, unmoving sea, and also plain drinking water that is not sparkling, still present in the flask.

clue.text: In great difficulty, but the flag is still flying

definitions.meaning: British slang for being in trouble
a flag still hoisted is at the top of its staff

explanation.surface: Things look bad, but the flag still flies.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for being in a mess, and literally a flag hoisted to the top of its staff.

clue.text: How the undisputed victor wins and passes on

definitions.meaning: to win easily, without effort
to hand something down to the next generation

explanation.surface: A clear winner triumphs and then hands over the title.
explanation.definitionFit: To win with ease, and to bequeath or hand on to heirs.

clue.text: One time, one-time

definitions.meaning: on a single occasion
former, as in a one-time champion

explanation.surface: A single occasion, or a former one.
explanation.definitionFit: On a single occasion, and also formerly, at some past time.

clue.text: Inclined to be making inventories

definitions.meaning: a ship leaning to one side
writing down items one by one

explanation.surface: A clerk is keen to draw up stock records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclined to be' reads as 'disposed to'; 'Inclined' is a ship leaning over.
explanation.definitionFit: A tilting ship leans over, and compiling inventories is drawing up catalogues of items.

clue.text: A few, less than a few, in fact anybody

parts.note: some means a few
a single one is fewer than a few

explanation.surface: Some, or even just one, really anybody at all.
explanation.walkthrough: SOME plus ONE; 'in fact' only joins the parts to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An unspecified person, any individual at all.

clue.text: Book a player unlikely to play

definitions.meaning: to book is to secure a seat or table in advance
a substitute held back from the team

explanation.surface: A team books a substitute who will probably sit on the bench.
explanation.definitionFit: To make an advance booking, and a substitute player kept back on the bench.

clue.text: One of those colours he got for sports?

definitions.text: One of those colours he got for sports?

parts.words: One of those colours he got for sports?
parts.note: at Oxford and Cambridge an athlete who represents the university is awarded colours named after a shade

explanation.surface: Someone asks which colour a sportsman was given.
explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge, sporting representatives are awarded a colour, dark for Oxford and light for Cambridge, so 'colours' are an honour, not paint.
explanation.definitionFit: An Oxbridge sportsman who represents his university wins a full honour named for the shade of sky.

clue.text: Postman contrived to hide the fifth letter twice to examine it surreptitiously

indicators.note: contrived means artificially arranged, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as letters to be rearranged

indicators.note: twice means the letter is used two times

parts.note: E is the fifth letter of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A nosy postman sneakily reads someone's letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to hide' says the two Es go in among the letters of POSTMAN, and 'contrived' rearranges the lot. 'letter' is the alphabet's, not the post's.
explanation.definitionFit: Using kettle vapour to loosen an envelope's glue lets one read a letter secretly.

clue.text: Not at home to the bowling?

definitions.meaning: away from the house
a cricket batsman dismissed by a bowler

explanation.surface: Someone is away from home at a bowling match.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batsman dismissed by the bowler is said to be this 'to the bowling'.
explanation.definitionFit: Absent from home, and dismissed in cricket by a bowler.

clue.text: Old road used for helicopter landing

definitions.meaning: an archaic word for a path or track
a flat area where helicopters touch down

explanation.surface: A disused old road is now a landing spot for helicopters.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a footpath, and the flat platform where helicopters touch down.

clue.text: Card game for well off circle

parts.note: well off read as a long way off, distant
O is circle-shaped

explanation.surface: A card game suits the wealthy social circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well off' looks like 'rich' but means a long way away. FARO is an old gambling card game.
explanation.definitionFit: A gambling game with cards, popular in the American West.

clue.text: Obviously second best way to go if you want to outdo the others

definitions.text: Obviously second best way to go if you want to outdo the others

parts.words: Obviously second best way to go if you want to outdo the others
parts.note: the idiom go ___ means to outdo; read literally, a single improvement sounds like coming only second best

explanation.surface: Someone advises that to beat rivals you need only modest improvement.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for outdoing someone is to 'go' this phrase; read as one step above, it sounds like a lowly ranking.
explanation.definitionFit: To go a step further than a rival is to surpass them, the idiom's sense.

clue.text: Central part of whole Ireland

indicators.note: central part of says the letters sit in the middle of the phrase that follows

explanation.surface: Someone describes the heart of all Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Central' as the definition, which it cannot be; the clue is all-in-one: the letters straddle 'wholE IREland', and the word is Ireland's own name for itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish-language name for the country, which takes up most of the island.

clue.text: Drew — string tight?

definitions.meaning: finished level in a match
string pulled tight in a knot has been knotted

explanation.surface: Someone drew a string tight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drew' suggests pulling; it is the sporting result of a level game.
explanation.definitionFit: Finishing level in a game, and fastened with a knot.

clue.text: Something with which to wind up Scottish festivities

definitions.text: Something with which to wind up
definitions.meaning: a spool on which thread or line is wound
a lively Scottish dance

explanation.surface: Something to close the Scottish celebrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wind up' suggests finishing the party; it means winding line on a spool.
explanation.definitionFit: A spool for winding fishing line or film, and a lively Scottish country dance.

clue.text: Sort of 'wolves apparently extinct?

definitions.meaning: the prefix for the mythical man-wolves
the past tense of are, so things no longer existing

explanation.surface: A kind of wolf appears to have died out.
explanation.walkthrough: The first part completes 'werewolves'; the second is the past tense of 'are', as if they no longer exist.
explanation.definitionFit: The prefix for shape-shifting man-wolves, and the past form of 'are', suggesting things no longer around.

clue.text: Certainly not Certainly not credit

parts.note: never is an emphatic no
never again, an emphatic no

explanation.surface: Someone refuses twice to buy on credit.
explanation.walkthrough: The British slang for hire purchase, buying on instalments, is the doubled phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for hire purchase, paying for goods in instalments.
